newsitem.title: USA: Another look at insurance as an investment.
newsitem.headline: Another look at insurance as an investment.

text.p: For many years, we financial writers have been saying that insurance is never an investment.

"Buy term, and invest the rest" has been our credo. Once you start mixing up your investment dollars with your insurance dollars, you become so mired in extra fees and incomprehensible policy illustrations you are lucky to get anything back. (Or unlucky, if you really think about what winning in life insurance entails.)

Now some new products are making us rethink those absolutes. For some time, variable annuities, which allow you to invest money for retirement on a tax deferred basis, have been coming down in price and going up in performance and demonstrating themselves worthwhile, particularly in high tax states.
Now, there are a few life insurance plans that combine low investment fees with insurance tax breaks in a package that, at least on the surface, looks enticing.

One that is notable is the Ameritas Low-Load Variable Universal Life policy. This programme combines low fees with solid investment choices, and you can buy it direct without a broker, insurance agent or commissions.
Donald Reiser, who as president of the Ameritas subsidiary selling this product, is its chief promoter, claims this is a great way to save for retirement. Is it?
It may be, if you like complicated prospectuses, don't mind bending a product to fit a shape for which it may not be intended, and can live with a little risk. Consider the details.

Reiser points out that you can buy a life insurance policy such as this one, pay minimal fees, invest most of your money through the policy in the stock market, and build a substantial nest egg without paying any income taxes on the proceeds.
When you retire, you can withdraw the money you've put in, upon which you've already been taxed, without paying added taxes on it. Then what?

Reiser suggests you borrow against the plan to fund your retirement. As long as you leave enough money in the plan to keep it in force, you may never pay taxes on the money you take out. When you die, the policy's death benefit will pass to your heirs tax free. This is a brilliant tax avoidance plan, right?
Maybe yes, maybe no. Consider these caveats:

-- Congress taketh, and Congress... "If word leaks out to Congress that people are borrowing right and left to fund their retirements, Congress would shut that down," suggests Morningstar insurance expert Jennifer Strickland. You're betting your nest egg on Congress continuing to give insurance products a free ride that nobody else gets.

-- It's cheap, but it's not free. Even in this rock-bottom programme, there's a 3.5 percent insurance tax, a 0.75 percent annual mortality charge, a monthy administrative fee that might run $9 and the management fees of the investments you select. Plus the cost of the insurance. Not worth the price if you don't need the insurance, too, says Strickland.

-- Don't forget about that "lapse in policy" clause. Like all insurance products, it's possible for your investment returns to fall below expectations. If they fall below what it costs to keep your policy in force, your policy can lapse, reports New York financial advisor Albert Golly. That can be bad, requiring you to send in more money in a hurry to keep the policy in force, or forcing you to pay taxes on loans already received out of the policy.

-- Overfunding's not a good idea, either. If you try to shelter too much in a programme like this, and keep the death benefit low so the policy doesn't ever lapse, you can get into a different kind of trouble. The IRS can determine that you're not buying an insurance policy, you're buying a modified endowment contract. Then you'll end up paying tax on the first dollar coming out of the policy and possibly paying penalties, too.

-- How much do those loans cost? When you borrow against an insurance policy, the company sets aside an equal amount of money in the policy in a safe place earning a low rate of interest, such as 4 percent. It then charges you interest on the loan. The interest that you pay may be higher than the amount your money is earning. If you are paying 6 percent, for example, you are paying 4 percent to yourself and 2 percent to Ameritas. And if you don't make your interest payments, they compound on themselves. So you end up paying interest on interest.

In the Ameritas plan, policyholders who have 10 years in the programme and are at least 55 can borrow up to 10 percent of their available cash at a "zero net" rate. That means their rate will be the same that the money in their account is earning, and the borrowing will cost them nothing. Except the lost opportunity of having their money in higher paying investments.

-- Are you willing to buy stocks? There's not a life insurance or variable annuity product that really works well unless you're willing to put the bulk of your investments in it into the stock market. The fees associated with these products tend to wipe out the lower yields on bonds and guaranteed investments.
The bottom line? It's impossible to generalize.

If you're in a high tax bracket, have the money to invest and need the insurance, you could probably do worse. But you might choose to invest first in a good actuary or accountant who could compare the life insurance plan with other retirement savings vehicles at your disposal. And keep rooting for the insurance lobby.
